units.text: If we melt ice, the world after melting seems to have different rules. A rigid object has become a liquid. We can attribute the change to temperature and collective state without assuming fundamental interactions were rewritten. This is the first, common and important sense in which ‘new laws appear’: the domain and effective description change.

The second sense concerns parameters. A relationship may retain the same form, but a quantity we considered constant may depend on time, location or an unknown field. In a broader theory, what was a fixed parameter can become a dynamical variable. We have not eliminated the idea of law; we have moved the boundary between rule and state.

Searches concerning the constancy of fundamental quantities are genuine physical research. Atomic-clock comparisons, spectral observations and other systems allow variations to be tested with different sensitivities and systematic errors. Uzan surveys both methods and the need for coherent theoretical frameworks to interpret results. This literature does not identify variation with proof of simulation (Uzan, 2011) .

One technical detail has enormous philosophical importance: we measure ratios. If we say a dimensional constant ‘changed its value’, we must specify units and standards. A unit change can change the written number without changing the world. Dimensionless quantities, such as certain ratios and dimensionless constants, avoid this direct ambiguity (Uzan, 2007) .

Return to the two imaginary clocks. If both accelerated by exactly the same ratio, together with every process through which we observe and remember, we would have no unchanged internal standard against which to detect the acceleration. If one changes its rate relative to the other, there is a measurable difference. An experiment has no access to ‘time outside the universe’ merely because we call an instrument a clock.

The third sense of change would be more radical: the fundamental rule itself would change. But we can immediately ask whether the modification follows another rule. If so, we have a metalaw. If not, we must explain what ‘follows no rule’ means and how we would distinguish this from a rule we do not yet know.

A universe in which parameter k increases according to k(t) = k₀ + at is not a lawless universe. It has a richer rule than k = constant. A universe in which k is modified by an external operator would have uncontrolled inputs from its internal perspective. But the operator’s behavior might itself be regular, random, goal-dependent or entirely opaque to observers.

Thus, ‘laws evolve’ is not yet an explanation. We must specify what evolves, relative to which time, through what mechanism and with what consequences. Otherwise we move the mystery from one noun to another. An explanation of change presupposing a possibility space, update rules and a probability measure already has a lawlike structure it must acknowledge.

There are also hypotheses attempting to explain why we observe particular parameter values. In a hypothetical ensemble of different regions or universes, observers would appear only under conditions compatible with their existence. This observational selection may matter but does not itself produce the ensemble or establish how probable its variants are. Saying ‘we had to observe a world in which we can exist’ is less than explaining that world’s mechanism.

Lee Smolin proposed cosmological natural selection: in a speculative scenario, black holes give birth to descendant universes with parameter variations. Universes producing more black holes would have more descendants. The analogy tries to replace arbitrary choice of constants with a mechanism of variation and reproduction. It is not a confirmed observation of universes being born or proof that life is the cosmos’s purpose (Smolin, 2006) .

The dispute shows why precision matters even in speculative research. In a 2006 critique, Vilenkin argues that changing the cosmological constant could increase black-hole production, contradicting the invoked optimization criterion. Smolin responds by challenging the physical assumptions used in that argument. We cannot turn this controversy into an experimental verdict on universe reproduction. We can see, however, that a hypothesis gains content when it produces a constraint and critics can say exactly where it would fail (Vilenkin, 2006; Smolin, 2006) .

In such scenarios, effective laws can have a genealogy. But the mechanism of generation, variation and selection itself presupposes rules. The problem is displaced and may become more precise without disappearing. A mechanism for the emergence of constants would be a major discovery even if it did not explain why the possibility space itself exists. Partial explanation is not useless merely because the ultimate question remains open.

We can also conceive a situation with no simple ultimate level. The world might allow successive descriptions without an available final foundation. This is a metaphysical possibility, not an established conclusion of physics. Likewise, a very simple fundamental structure may exist while we cannot prove there is no deeper one.

What would living with this uncertainty mean? Not nervously checking gravity at every step. Practical confidence must relate to evidence and the domains where it works. But neither should we declare an anomaly impossible merely because it would contradict the textbook. Textbooks are documents about knowledge, not contracts signed by the universe.

A law can be revised for three very different reasons: we measured incorrectly; we discovered the domain was narrower; we found different dynamics. Only the last could support certain senses of profound physical change, and even it does not automatically identify an external author. When we say ‘nature changed its rules’, we must be sure we are not merely describing the moment we understood them better.
